item.title: Kanagawa at New Year: Kawasaki Daishi, the Hakone Ekiden & a Day-by-Day Plan
item.description: Kanagawa has the busiest New Year in Japan, and most visitors to Tokyo never realise it. Kawasaki Daishi draws around three million worshippers in the first three days of January, putting it among the two or three most-visited temples in the country. Tsurugaoka Hachimangu in Kamakura takes over two million more. And on January 2 and 3, the Hakone Ekiden — the relay race that stops the nation — runs its entire course through this prefecture, from the Kawasaki waterfront to the shore of Lake Ashi and back.

item.title: Kyoto at New Year: Okera-mairi, Temple Bells & a Day-by-Day Plan
item.description: Kyoto at New Year does something no other Japanese city manages: it keeps its temples and gardens open while the rest of the country shuts, and it adds rituals that have been performed on these exact streets for a thousand years. On the night of December 31, people queue at Yasaka Shrine to catch a sacred flame on a length of braided rope, then walk it home through the dark to light the first soup of the year.

item.title: Mie at New Year: Ise Jingu Hatsumode, Meoto Iwa Sunrise & a Day-by-Day Plan
item.description: Mie has the most serious New Year in Japan. Ise Jingu is not simply a popular shrine — it is the shrine, the home of Amaterasu, the sun goddess from whom the imperial line claims descent, and the spiritual centre of Shinto. In the first days of January it receives worshippers in the millions, with something like half a million crossing the Uji Bridge on January 1 alone. For centuries, before trains existed, ordinary people saved for years to walk here; that sense of a once-in-a-lifetime pilgrimage has never entirely gone.

item.title: Osaka at New Year: Sumiyoshi Taisha, Toka Ebisu & a Day-by-Day Plan
item.description: Osaka is the easiest of Japan’s big cities to visit at New Year, and the reason is simple: this is a city built on commerce and eating out, so a far higher share of its restaurants, arcades and food stalls trade straight through the holiday than in Kyoto or Tokyo. It is also the city with the loudest New Year in Japan — not on January 1, but on January 9–11, when something close to a million people pour into Imamiya Ebisu Shrine to buy a bamboo branch hung with gold coins and ask, with total frankness, for a profitable year.

item.title: Tokyo at New Year: Hatsumode, What's Closed & a Day-by-Day Plan
item.description: New Year (oshogatsu, お正月) is the most important holiday in Japan, and it is the one period when visiting Tokyo is genuinely different from visiting Tokyo at any other time. Not harder — different. The city empties of residents who travel to family homes, trains run half-full, the air is cold and unusually clear, and for a few days the world’s largest metropolis feels almost provincial. Then, at the shrines, the entire country shows up at once.

item.title: Japan 3 Week Spring Itinerary with Tohoku Region
item.description: Japan 3 Week Itinerary Including Tohoku: The Ultimate 21-Day Route From Tokyo to the Deep North and Back Most visitors to Japan follow the well-worn Tokyo–Kyoto–Osaka route, maybe adding Hiroshima or Nara for good measure. That’s a wonderful trip, but it misses something essential: the soul of old Japan that still breathes quietly in the northern Tohoku region. This Japan 3 week itinerary including Tohoku fixes that. Over 21 days, you’ll experience the electric energy of Tokyo, the cultural depth of Kyoto, the street food paradise of Osaka, the sobering history of Hiroshima — and then head north into a Japan that most foreign visitors never see, where mountain temples sit in cedar forests, hot spring towns hide in volcanic valleys, and local grandmothers serve you the best bowl of noodles you’ve ever had.

item.title: Japan Autumn Itinerary: 14-Day Fall Foliage Route
item.description: Japan Autumn Itinerary 14 Days: The Ultimate Fall Foliage Route From Tokyo to Kyushu Introduction: Why Autumn Is Japan’s Best-Kept Secret Season If you’ve ever scrolled through photos of crimson maple tunnels, golden ginkgo-lined avenues, and misty mountain temples draped in fire-colored leaves, you already understand why autumn in Japan is magical. What you might not know is that a well-planned Japan autumn itinerary 14 days long can take you through the full spectrum of fall — from the alpine peaks where colors arrive in late September to the southern temples where momiji (maple viewing) lingers into early December.

item.title: Japan Food Tour Guide 2026: Tokyo, Osaka, Kyoto
item.description: Japan Food Tour Itinerary 10 Days: Tokyo, Osaka & Kyoto — The Ultimate Eating Journey If you’ve ever dreamed of eating your way across Japan, let me tell you — ten days is the sweet spot. Not so short that you’re rushing between cities, not so long that your budget (or belt) can’t handle it. A well-planned Japan food tour itinerary 10 days covering Tokyo, Osaka, and Kyoto lets you experience three radically different food cultures, each shaped by centuries of local tradition, geography, and seasonal obsession.

item.title: Japan Food Tour: 10 Days of Best Eats Spring
item.description: Japan Food Tour Itinerary 10 Days Best Eats: The Ultimate Guide to Eating Your Way Across Japan Introduction: Why This Japan Food Tour Itinerary Will Change How You Travel If you’ve been dreaming about a Japan food tour itinerary 10 days best eats style—where every city, every meal, and every snack tells a story—this is the guide I wish I’d had when I first moved to Japan fifteen years ago.

item.title: Japan Hidden Gems: 10 Days Winter Adventure Off the Beaten Path
item.description: Japan Off the Beaten Path Itinerary: 14 Days of Hidden Destinations Most Tourists Never See If you’ve already done Tokyo, Kyoto, and Osaka — or if you’re a first-timer who wants to skip the crowds entirely — this Japan off the beaten path itinerary is built for you. Over 14 days, you’ll travel through hidden destinations that don’t appear in most guidebooks: fishing villages where grandmothers still dive for abalone, mountain towns where sake breweries have operated for centuries, volcanic islands with wild horses, and valleys so remote they were once called “the Tibet of Japan.

item.title: Japan in November 2026 Autumn Leaves Itinerary
item.description: Japan in November Autumn Leaves Itinerary: The Ultimate Guide to Koyo Season Introduction: Why November Is Japan’s Most Magical Month There’s a moment in early November when something shifts across the Japanese archipelago. The maples begin to burn—not with fire, but with a slow, breathtaking crescendo of crimson, amber, and gold that sweeps southward from the mountain peaks to the temple gardens below. After fifteen years of living in Japan, I can tell you without hesitation: November is the single best month to visit this country.

item.title: Japan Spring Cherry Blossom 14 Day Itinerary
item.description: Japan 2 Week Itinerary Spring Cherry Blossom Season: The Ultimate 14-Day Guide (2025) Spring in Japan is not just a season—it’s a collective exhale. After months of cold gray skies, the entire country turns its face toward the pale pink blossoms that sweep northward like a slow-motion wave. If you’re planning a Japan 2 week itinerary spring cherry blossom season, you’re chasing one of the most beautiful natural phenomena on Earth, and two weeks gives you the rare luxury of seeing it unfold across multiple cities.
